title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
Charging from zero
Starting from 0 V toward a supply \(V_s\):
\[
V(t) = V_s \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)
\]
Discharging back toward 0 V from \(V_s\) follows the mirror image, \(V(t) = V_s e^{-t/\tau}\).

title: Ohm’s law and power
text: The relationship every other circuit identity gets built on top of.

title: Ohm’s law and power
text:
The law
For a resistor, voltage and current are proportional:
\[
V = IR
\]
Power dissipated follows from \(P = VI\), substituted with Ohm’s law to give two more useful forms:
\[
P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
\]
The \(I^2R\) form is the one that matters for sizing: double the current through a fixed resistance and dissipation quadruples, not doubles — a common reason parts run hotter than expected after a “small” current increase.

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Loaded divider
Once something draws current from the output node — an ADC input, another circuit — that load resistor \(R_L\) sits in parallel with \(R_2\), and the divider ratio changes:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2 \| R_L}{R_1 + (R_2 \| R_L)}, \qquad R_2 \| R_L = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}
\]
This is why a divider that measures correctly open-circuit can read low once connected to a real load — the rule of thumb is to keep \(R_L \gg R_2\), typically 10× or more.

title: About
text:
I’m a hardware engineer, and on any given day I might be reading about magnetics, debugging an IC datasheet, tuning a microcontroller peripheral, or writing the software that ties it all together. For a long time the notes from that ended up scattered across notebooks and apps on different devices, half-findable at best.
This site is where those notes live now — one place, organized by topic, with the math written out rather than just the result. Most pages carry a small calculator next to the derivation, so a formula isn’t just something to read but something to actually use on a real design.
It’s a running project: chapters get added as I work through new topics, and existing notes get revised as I learn more or find a cleaner way to derive something.

title: Buck-boost converter
text: The classic (inverting) buck-boost can step the output above or below the input, at the cost of an inverted polarity — the output is referenced negative to the input’s ground. Same ideal CCM treatment as the buck and boost pages.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
\frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in}} = \frac{D}{1-D} \quad \Rightarrow \quad D = \frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in} + |V_{out}|}
\]
\(D < 0.5\) steps down, \(D > 0.5\) steps up — the same switch duty cycle range covers both directions, which is the whole appeal of the topology.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Inductor current
The inductor is charged from \(V_{in}\) only, during the on-time — same charging behavior as a boost:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
And the output only sees current during the off-time, so — again like a boost —
\[
I_{L,avg} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]
This is the least efficient of the three topologies in practice: the inductor carries both the input and output current duty cycles, so RMS current (and core/copper loss) tends to be the highest of the three for a given output power.

title: LC and RC filter design
text: The two filters you reach for constantly: a simple RC low-pass for signal-level filtering, and an LC low-pass for power-stage or EMI filtering where you can’t afford a resistor’s power loss.

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
RC low-pass
A single resistor and capacitor to ground give a first-order (−20 dB/decade) low-pass with cutoff:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}
\]
Simple, but the resistor dissipates power continuously — fine for a signal line, not for filtering a DC-DC converter’s output current.

Calculator

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
LC low-pass
Replacing the resistor with an inductor removes the continuous power loss — the standard choice at a converter’s output or as an input EMI filter. Second-order (−40 dB/decade) response:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}
\]
For a target cutoff, there’s a free parameter — usually chosen via the filter’s characteristic impedance \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}\), which should roughly match the source/load impedance to avoid ringing:
\[
L = \frac{Z_0}{2\pi f_c}, \qquad C = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c Z_0}
\]
A too-low \(Z_0\) makes for a large capacitor and a peaky, underdamped response without added series resistance; too high makes for a large, lossy inductor. Real designs also check the \(Q\) at \(f_c\) against the source/load resistance and add damping if it rings.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text: A quick derivation of solenoid inductance from first principles, then the practical correction engineers actually use, with a calculator to try real turn counts and dimensions.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
The ideal case
Treating the coil as infinitely long, Ampere’s law gives a uniform field inside: \(B = \mu_0 n I\), where \(n = N / l\) is turns per unit length. Flux linkage through all \(N\) turns gives:
\[
L_{ideal} = \mu_0 N^2 \frac{\pi r^2}{l}
\]
This overestimates inductance for any real, finite coil — it ignores fringing at the ends.



Fig. 1 — field concentrated inside the winding, with fringing paths returning outside.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
Wheeler’s correction
For a real single-layer coil where length isn’t much greater than radius, Wheeler’s 1928 approximation is the standard practical formula (\(r\), \(l\) in inches, result in \(\mu H\)):
\[
L_{\mu H} \approx \frac{r^2 N^2}{9r + 10l}
\]
Valid roughly for \(l > 0.4r\). Below that, it undercorrects and a full Nagaoka-coefficient treatment is needed.



Fig. 2 — field strength rising with current, fringing appearing at the ends.

title: Buck converter
text: A buck converter steps a DC input down to a lower DC output by switching an inductor between the input and ground, then filtering the result. This is the ideal, continuous-conduction-mode (CCM) analysis — enough to pick a starting inductor and output capacitor.

title: Buck converter
text:
Duty cycle
Ignoring losses, the output is set entirely by duty cycle:
\[
D = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Inductor selection
While the switch is on, the inductor sees \((V_{in} - V_{out})\) across it for time \(D/f_{sw}\); while off, it sees \(-V_{out}\) for \((1-D)/f_{sw}\). Either way gives the same ripple current:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{out}(1 - D)}{f_{sw} L}
\]
Solving for \(L\) at a target ripple (commonly 20–40% of \(I_{out}\)):
\[
L = \frac{V_{out}(1-D)}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Output capacitor
Assuming the ripple is dominated by capacitance (not ESR), the output voltage ripple is approximately:
\[
\Delta V_{out} \approx \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, C_{out}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_{out} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, \Delta V_{out}}
\]
Real capacitors also add ESR-driven ripple (\(\Delta V_{ESR} = \Delta I_L \cdot R_{ESR}\)) on top of this — worth checking separately against the datasheet ESR once a part is chosen.

title: Boost converter
text: A boost converter steps a DC input up to a higher DC output by storing energy in an inductor while a switch is closed, then dumping it into the output (through a diode or synchronous switch) once it opens. Ideal CCM analysis again.

title: Boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
D = 1 - \frac{V_{in}}{V_{out}}
\]

title: Boost converter
text:
Inductor current
While the switch is on, the full input voltage sits across the inductor, so ripple current is:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
Unlike a buck, the inductor carries the input current, not the output current — this is why boost converters need bulkier inductors for the same output power. By power balance (\(V_{in}I_{in} = V_{out}I_{out}\), ideal):
\[
I_{L,avg} = I_{in} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Parallel
Resistors in parallel share the same voltage, and their currents add, giving a reciprocal sum:
\[
\frac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}
\]
The parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor — adding a path for current can only make it easier for current to flow.

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
Series RLC magnitude
For R, L, and C in series, the reactances subtract (they’re 180° apart) before combining with resistance:
\[
|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}
\]
This hits a minimum, \(|Z| = R\), at the resonant frequency where \(X_L = X_C\).
